I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette:
Rodrigo Castellanos is a 54-year-old Colombian-American man who built a mid-sized logistics company from the ground up over three decades, a business that now employs forty-two people and occupies most of his waking hours. He is married, the father of two adult children, and by most external measures a man who has navigated difficulty successfully. He presented for therapy eight weeks ago, describing himself as "finally out of excuses" for not seeking help sooner.

Seven years ago, Rodrigo volunteered through a faith-based humanitarian organization to spend six months coordinating supply chains for a relief operation in a conflict-affected region of Central America. He had done similar work before, shorter deployments to calmer zones, and believed his practical experience would be an asset. What he had not anticipated was the degree to which the front lines had migrated into the areas where his team operated. Approximately three months into the deployment, his convoy was ambushed on a rural road. The vehicle ahead of his was hit. Rodrigo's driver stopped abruptly and Rodrigo stepped out, instinctively, to assess the situation - and found himself standing in the open as gunfire erupted around him. A colleague was struck and fell within arm's reach of him. Rodrigo pulled the man behind the vehicle and pressed his hands against the wound, remaining there for what he later estimated was twenty minutes, though he could not be certain. The colleague survived. Rodrigo returned home four weeks later, telling his wife he was fine, telling himself the same thing.

The months that followed were quiet in a way that unsettled him without his fully understanding why. By the end of the first year, certain things had become intolerable. The sound of a car backfiring, a firecracker, anything percussive and sudden would send him back to that road - not as a memory he could observe from a distance, but as something happening now, in his body and behind his eyes. He began to structure his life around avoiding public events where such sounds might occur. Fourth of July celebrations, which his family had always attended together, became something he refused to discuss. His wife learned not to push.

At his warehouse, where deliveries arrive throughout the day and workers move in tight corridors, the physical closeness of other bodies had become its own problem. When a staff member approached him unexpectedly from behind, or when a meeting crowded too many people into a small room, something in him would lock and harden. He began holding all staff meetings in his largest conference room, always positioning himself near the door, and his employees had quietly noticed the change in him without knowing what to name it.

What confused Rodrigo most - and what he described with particular difficulty in early sessions - was what happened on good days. When his business closed a strong contract, when he laughed genuinely with his wife over dinner, when something simply felt pleasant, he would find himself almost immediately suspicious of the feeling, as though joy were a form of inattention he could not afford. He had come to believe, without quite articulating it, that feeling well was dangerous, a signal that he had let his guard down.

He had begun carrying a licensed firearm, something he had never done before the deployment. He told himself it was practical, that a business owner with his responsibilities had reasons to be cautious, but he knew the reasoning was thinner than he let on. He also knew that in the past two years he had begun manufacturing conflict - with vendors, with his wife over small things, with a longtime business partner over a disagreement that could have been resolved in an afternoon. He was certain, in a way he struggled to explain, that the friction kept something worse at bay.

He had also spent years cycling through the same questions: why he had been the one standing in the open, why that convoy, why that day, as though an answer existed somewhere that would make the whole thing cohere.

What finally brought Rodrigo to therapy was his wife's quiet statement one evening that she missed him - not that she was angry, just that she missed him. He arrived at the first session hoping, above all, to understand what had happened to the man he used to be.
